speaker: The Chairman
text: Head L, Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In recent years, the concept of zero waste has been growing in popularity all over the world.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In land-scarce Singapore, zero waste is even more critical.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Building another landfill by the 2030s is not possible.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The most practicable long-term solution, therefore, is to reduce waste.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has taken the lead with education, as well as funding of technology and research and development (R&D), to promote eco-friendly waste management.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: That is a big step forward, but this support has not been translated into action.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As individuals, we can do our part by reducing consumption.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When we generate waste, we should dispose of it appropriately.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But some people treat them like trash bins, contaminating them with food waste, soiled garments and so on.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What can we do to get more Singaporeans to recycle properly?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we include domestic helpers and foreign workers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They play a big role at home and at work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What is the Ministry doing to reach out to these groups to help get them on the same page?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we do more to improve the heartland recycling network?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Moving on to businesses, I note several have taken the initiative to reduce plastic use.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some food and beverage (F&B) businesses no longer provide straws, for example.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: All these bode well, but more can be done.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Government take a more proactive approach, including identifying companies that should have a waste reduction programme, working closely with them to help them turn it into something beneficial?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some companies do not know the range of solutions possible and assume that recycling would be troublesome and time-wasting and, hence, may be reluctant to take part.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A little motivation with some handholding and incentives in the initial stage could help to get things moving.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some have even gone a step further to create a business out of a potential solution.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Customers would pay a fee for these items and get their money back when they return them at a nearby location.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It frees businesses from the labour cost of hiring dish washers and resolves the problem of facilitating takeouts without using disposables.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Government incentivise such businesses and work with them to refine their ideas for mass uptake?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On the other hand, this possibly leads to a dilemma.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These cutlery and containers would have to be washed, so water consumption goes up.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Essentially, when we reuse something, we usually must maintain its cleanliness.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How do we balance the effort to reduce plastic disposables with our need to save water?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: While on this subject, I am aware that our Public Utilities Board (PUB) has always been putting in a lot of effort on technology and R&D to secure our water supply.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What are the new developments in the water sector that we can look forward to?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In what ways can technology be used to optimise the way in which the Ministry and PUB operate?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In recent weeks, we have heard the price of water being mentioned again and again by one of our old suppliers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have also launched a water conservation campaign at home.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As a small, low-lying island-state, we need to be aware of how climate change impacts us.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have experienced more frequent and more extreme weather events.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have had our share of flash floods and scorching hot sun.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To effectively tackle climate change, it is necessary for us to work with other countries.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How are we doing in terms of regional and international engagements?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are also several tropical island states that could face similar challenges.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are we working with them on a solution?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What about the myriad of tiny islets that belong to our nation?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We are made up of 63 islands altogether.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How are we protecting them from climate change?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We designated last year as the Year of Climate Action.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How will the Ministry continue the efforts from the Year of Climate Action?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What are the key climate-related initiatives that we can look forward to this year and beyond?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In 2013, the Ministry established the Centre for Climate Research to develop climate projections for Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Its findings will guide us towards prioritising our key challenges and building up our resilience.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What more will the Ministry do to continue to build up our climate science capabilities to ensure that we are well-prepared against climate changes?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What are we doing to nurture an adequate local talent pool to implement the relevant technology and research programmes?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Let us all do our part so that our nation will not be submerged in water in years to come.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Every day, we are throwing away, on average, more than 2,000 tonnes of food.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The rest of the food waste is disposed of at incineration plants.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Food waste is a concern because food that we throw away, in essence, also amounts to wasting the resources used in its production as well as their treatment and disposal.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides wasting money, it also has negative environmental impact.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There have been ongoing efforts to collect and dispose of food waste.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By and large, there are four major strategies adopted by NEA.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the strategy of redistributing unsold and excess food, I feel that there is scope to do more.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We could involve more of the community groups to redistribute unsold or excess food to help needy families.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my constituency, for example, our Zhenghua Indian Activity Executive Committee does that every month, collecting food from wholesale market and redistributing it to needy residents at our estates.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By so doing, food unsold is not wasted and it can make a difference to low-income families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It signals the Government’s strong commitment towards protecting our environment and ensuring that we have sustainable practices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that the main emphasis of the Master Plan is on reducing our consumption rather than on recycling what we have used.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to focus on the root of the problem and address our throwaway culture.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we do not reduce our consumption and instead focus mainly on recycling, our efforts will be futile.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Equally important is public ownership of the Master Plan.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: People need to have a stake in it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And we can achieve this by ensuring that people’s views and ideas, from the green groups as well as the general public, are heard.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if the Master Plan is already completed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If not, will there be plans to consult the public, and when will they take place?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Quite simply, because I use a mobile phone and a laptop.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As recently as last month, a media report highlighted that "The critically endangered Grauer’s gorilla has lost 77% of its population in the last 20 years, partly due to the mining of minerals used to make cellphones." The mineral extracted and used is coltan.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share more details about this, whether it can be brought forward and also whether this can include the recycling of mobile phones and, in particular, the mineral coltan?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A few months ago, I delivered an Adjournment Motion, calling for us to move Towards a Plastic-Lite Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In that speech, I shared that a recent study found 1.8 trillion pieces of plastic, weighing a total of 80,000 tonnes, currently floating in a stretch of ocean between California and Hawaii.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we do not do anything about it, there will be more plastics than fish in our ocean by 2050.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share more details about this, whether there will be mandatory reduction targets set and whether there will be any measures to ensure that businesses have significant plans for reduction?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One of the places where a lot of disposables are used is at our hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A lot of people take away their food and disposables are used since it is still rare that people bring their own containers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to tackle this issue, but what we should tackle first is the use of disposables for dining in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This has clearly resulted in a significant drop in the amount of waste generated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If not, will the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources (MEWR) consider providing incentives or subsidies for hawkers who choose not to use disposables for dining in?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do understand that disposables are used, as it is more convenient and may be cheaper.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, providing such incentives might encourage hawkers to make this change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a call to action that I fully support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also a call to action that the Public Service, the biggest employer in Singapore, should support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Public agencies currently follow the procurement principles of fairness, transparency and value-for-money.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can environmental sustainability also be included in these principles?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even with a healthy economy, there will be no future if we do not have a healthy environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the words of Mdm Ho Ching, "There is, as you know, no Plan B for us, because there is no Planet B."

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe the focus will be on upstream solutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister for Finance has exhorted Singaporeans as individuals to change our way of life and practise the 3Rs – to Reduce consumption, Recycle and Reuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I would like to warn against neglecting what may be seen as downstream issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The 3Rs are not simply linked to individual ways of life that could be easily changed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ways of life are bound up with social norms, cultural beliefs and urban systems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The blue bins at each block of flats have hit a green ceiling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On reducing, we have to tackle head-on the rise of new patterns of retail and consumption.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The rise of home delivery and online shopping means packaging waste will only get higher.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On reusing, many countries are now promoting the reusing of waste for building and construction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is MEWR working with the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) on this front to promote the reusing of waste by our construction companies for their projects?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I wish to call attention to the management of medication wastage in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As we are aware, escalating healthcare cost is a great concern for Singapore's Budget.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, imperative to use the resources given to us as efficiently as possible.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As we continue to ramp up our healthcare system with more infrastructure, manpower, funding and subsidy schemes to cater to the needs of our ageing population, active steps must also be taken to review the waste in our current healthcare system.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This year, I understand that in Zero Waste, Singapore will be looking into food waste, plastic disposable waste, recycling efforts and business waste.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It does not, however, include medication waste in its initiative.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would like to declare my interest as the President of the Pharmaceutical Society of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore faces a rapidly ageing population and, as a consequence, patients with more chronic diseases.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: It is then inevitable that polypharmacy, which is the concurrent use of multiple medications by a patient, overprescribing and oversupply have been identified to be significant sources of medication waste.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: From past home visits by pharmacists to review the medications of patients, high medication waste was noted largely due to expired drugs, drugs prescribed without indication or duplication of drug therapy.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: A recent patient survey conducted by the NUS Pharmacy department and the National Cancer Centre Singapore over a two-week period, also revealed a resolution of patients' medical conditions, medication expired at home and patients no longer requiring their medications as top reasons for unused medications in their household.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Such medication hoarding translates to significant potential healthcare cost savings if we are able to curb the current issues of over-prescribing, oversupply and polypharmacy.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from incurring huge costs, over-prescribing, oversupplying and medication wastes also lead to issues of inappropriate medication disposal and environmental pollution.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Medication waste comprises of both hazardous and non-hazardous waste, controlled drug and expired pharmaceuticals.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, the most common way for individuals to dispose of medications is through the outlet of household waste.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Failure to ensure safe disposal of drugs can lead to environmental risks, as medicines which enter the environment can have a corrosive effect, especially on our local marine life.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This, in turn, will adversely affect other species.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that most wastewater treatment facilities cannot filter out these drugs.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: A case in point would be the potentially careless disposal of cytotoxic drugs, a group of medications that contain chemicals that are toxic to cells.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: They are used as part of chemotherapy regimens for cancer treatment.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: These drugs are also widely used in the treatment of other chronic diseases.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Cytotoxic drugs affect cell functions and have the ability to alter DNA and cause chromosome damage.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, they are teratogenic, carcinogenic and mutagenic in nature.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Antibiotics, if improperly discarded, can enter our ecosystem and promote resistance to bacteria and fungus, leading to increased rates of infections that are difficult to treat.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This is a vicious cycle which we cannot afford to risk happening and should be avoided at all costs.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Accidental drug overdose is also one of the most common sources of household injuries.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Young children are especially vulnerable to unintentional exposure to prescription and over-the-counter medications.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: As such, drugs should be safeguarded closely and gotten rid of safely when no longer needed.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Inappropriate disposal of drugs can also potentially lead to diversion for illicit use.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The potential savings from the earlier studies show considerable cost effectiveness of reimbursing a pharmacist for such services.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This take-back programme should be studied and implemented in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The Drug Enforcement Administration in the US created the National Prescription Drug take-back days that occur bi-annually in April and October.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: These take-back days are part of a mission to create safe medication disposal sites, prevent drug diversion or transfer of the prescribed drugs for illicit use, as well as to provide education for the public.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Our local survey mentioned above also show that our patients are supportive of such disposal sites.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: MOH and NEA may also consider collaboration with pharmacists to support patient education efforts in minimising medication waste.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: This is to prevent wastage in case of adverse effects, or if the medication proves unsuitable or ineffective.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: For medications taken on a "use when necessary" basis, to obtain them in small quantities and purchase more only when necessary.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: For example, to collect three months' worth of supply each time to minimise wastage.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For Singapore to achieve our vision of becoming a zero-waste nation, Singaporeans have to reduce our consumption and also adopt a zero‐waste attitude in their day‐to‐day life, such as stop using single‐use plastics.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Getting our recycling habits right is another way.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We have to increase our household recycling rate.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In my cuts for the Ministry of Education, I stressed the importance of inculcating our younger generation with green habits and lifestyle.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: After a discussion on Semakau Landfill, a young man went back to pick up the brochure he got when he visited Semakau as a student 10 years ago.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The trip made him more environmentally conscious, but it did not manage to make him feel the urgency to recycle or reduce waste!

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Every one of us has to take zero-waste and green lifestyle more seriously as a nation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We need to work together to extend the lifespan of the landfill, we must cut down our waste.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: So, it is important that we have a Zero Waste Master Plan.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I would like to ask the Minister how the public and other interested stakeholders can share their suggestions and ideas on how we can move towards on a zero-waste nation together.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister share more details on how we intend to implement the framework?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, we are physically small with a limited amount of land to install solar panels.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Singapore is surrounded by water and we also have reservoirs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Last year, it was reported that the Housing and Development Board (HDB) is exploring having floating solar panels in the open sea and that it is studying if such panels are suitable for our coastal marine conditions.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This year, we have a huge floating solar panel system coming up on our northern shores.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister provide an update on our floating solar plans?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Are there plans for PUB to deploy more solar panels at our reservoirs in the future?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Deloitte and InnoEnergy estimate that poor air quality in the European Union could cost €775 billion by 2020, based on premature deaths, healthcare costs and lower productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While we are all affected by regional air pollution from the haze, we may not realise that vehicle emissions also significantly affect local air quality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Conversion of our vehicle fleet to electric will reduce emissions, even after accounting for the fact that our electricity is generated by fossil fuels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Electrification of private cars will be challenging because there is little charging infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In any case, the best way to reduce emissions is to go car-lite.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Ministry support this plan to electrify the Government public service fleet by examining: (a) the impacts of particulates and other emissions from the vehicle fleet on health, quality of life and economic output; (b) the experiences of commercial providers of zero emissions transport, such as HDT or Blue SG, to understand barriers to widespread adoption; and (c) the related tax and subsidy policies needed to electrify major private vehicle fleets, such as private buses and taxis?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, it was announced last year that Singaporeans will have three new after-death facilities in the near future to meaningfully send off their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: A new facility for the scattering of ashes at sea without having to travel by boat is being built at Tanah Merah.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It was reported that there will be four pavilions accommodating seven people each and a shelter for 28 people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I have similar questions for the inland ash scattering facilities at Choa Chu Kang Cemetery Complex and the Mandai Crematorium and Columbarium Complex.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It was reported that these would be ready in 2020 and 2021 respectively.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Is the construction of the facilities on track for completion in the next two years?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We have been given some general information about the facilities being open to all faiths and are set in a beautiful, tranquil and respectful environment.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: But there are very few details about the facilities.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Will the Minister please share what the public can expect from the facilities?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Unlike the keeping of ashes in an urn in the Columbarium, the scattering of ashes is the last ceremony for family members to pay their last respects to the remains of their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: As such, it is important that the design of the facilities should be properly thought out and the facilities planning takes into account the comfort and privacy of grieving family members as well as accommodating the ritual requirements of the different faiths.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Ministry will share more information on the planned facilities and perhaps conduct a public consultation?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, in November 2018, I filed an oral Parliamentary Question (PQ) for the Minister for the Environment and Water Resources in respect of the supply of 8,600 quartz niches, instead of marble ones, when the niches were relocated from Mount Vernon Columbarium.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Specifically, I had asked: (a) whether NEA had verified that all contractual requirements have been fulfilled by the contractors during delivery and installation; (b) what punitive action will be taken against the contractors; and (c) whether the contractors are required to provide refunds or compensation where affected families do not accept a marble replacement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister clarify what was the explanation given by the contractor?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Was it a deliberate attempt on the part of the contractor?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There was no mention of any Police report or Police investigation in the PQ answer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a Police report was made, when was it made and whether any investigation was carried out or is being carried out by the Police or the Commercial Affairs Department?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Here are where we can get our three daily meals, or six, if you include brunch, tea and supper, from professionals offering cuisines from east to west at affordable prices.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is from our vibrant and unique hawker culture that the world’s first Michelin-starred street food stall emerged – "Hong Kong Soya Chicken Rice and Noodle" run by chef-owner Chan Hon Meng.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am sure that we will have more champions like Mr Chan in the future.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is because we have many hawker stalls which serve up delicious food reflecting our diverse cultural heritage and innovative fusions which can only be found here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our hawker centres are an important and intrinsic part of our history.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government, community and stakeholders must work together to ensure that this living legacy will continue to flourish.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What more can Singaporeans do to lend support?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Selling food is a tough and competitive business, even more so for hawkers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The work is physically demanding and the hours are long.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many Singaporeans are concerned that selling hawker food might become a dying trade with fewer younger people taking it up as a career.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry review and implement further measures to sustain our hawker trade and culture?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Part of the reason the younger generation is not so attracted to running hawker stalls is the availability of other food sale alternatives.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Those passionate about making food can choose to work for food courts run by chains, restaurants, hotels and catering firms.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They can earn decent salaries in better environments.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They can even operate their own eateries or restaurants with financial backers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, this also means that good, affordable food may not be so widely available in the future.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To ensure that we have a steady stream of younger hawkers, more has to be done to ensure a decent livelihood for our hawkers while keeping hawker food affordable for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are some hawkers who, despite having spent years in this trade, are less successful or who are even struggling.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there counsellors at the Ministry whom they can turn to for feedback and suggestions on how to turn their businesses around?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the success factors of hawkers doing well and how could these information and insights be shared with this group?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last but not least, our hawker centres need the cooperation of all customers to stay clean and pleasant for dining.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unfortunately, a minority of diners are not so neat when they eat and leave a mess of bones or unwanted food pieces on the tables.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we educate our people to be more considerate and hygienic?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can we improve our dining etiquette as a nation?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In view of the labour shortage for cleaning staff, Singaporeans have to get used to returning our own trays or, even better, like the Japanese, wipe and clean up our tables before we leave.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What further measures will the Ministry take to ensure the success of the tray return programme?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Currently, the Ministry has put in place measures to ensure that rentals are reasonable and not speculative.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: In this way, the interests of the hawkers are well-protected.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: The productivity solutions, such as centralised dishwashing and automated tray return systems, are steps in the right direction and help to ease our tight manpower situation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: I can see that the Ministry had attempted to strike a balance between the soft-touch regulatory approach towards SEHC operators and to exercise better oversight to protect hawkers' welfare.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: To that end, I welcome NEA's review of the key contractual terms between the SEHC operators and stallholders to provide more flexibility, while ensuring proper management.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: For example, operators will be more flexible on the stallholders’ operating hours and days of work required.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: To attract more to enter the hawker trade, we not only need to lower the barrier to entry but the barrier to exist as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Does the Ministry have updates on whether those measures have been effective?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Can you please take all the four together?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are even ahead of large agricultural nations, such as the US and Canada.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: According to the same Index, we are top chiefly because of affordability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This vulnerability is beyond just food cost but also our survival.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Food crises are not so distant in history.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The last global food crisis was a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In 2014, when Malaysian eggs were found to have salmonella, egg prices rose quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Clearly, food resilience must be a core national focus.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister share what are the key traits and supply risks that Singapore faces?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How have we been strengthening our food supplies in the face of geopolitical and economic developments?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By 2050, the world's population is expected to hit 10 billion from the current 7.3 billion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If we do not increase our agricultural yields massively over the next 30 years, the world will simply be in an economic growth-driven famine.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore's competition for food will only be keener.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is mission-critical to increase the local content of our food supplies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have diversified our food sources to manage our risk and food cost.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But only local production can protect us from short-term shocks and provide a measure of self-sufficiency.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What is the Ministry's target of local production to imported food supplies over the next 10 to 30 years?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Are we on our way to meeting this target?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the 1960s, agriculture accounted for 3% of our gross domestic product (GDP).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Has the Ministry set a target GDP rate?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For us to succeed in this national mission, both businesses and consumers play critical roles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Locally produced food will generally cost more than imported ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is no different from the higher cost of water produced by distillation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, if we do not see the value of food self-sufficiency as a national imperative, then there is no future for local production.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For once, we have to literally drink and eat our way to security or disaster.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, 40% of the eggs sold are from our local farms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Buying "local" also meant that FairPrice has a stronger control over quality and safety from farms to dining table.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They also started a small and medium size enterprise (SME) development and support programme to help 400 small companies and startups with their cash flow and development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It has committed to monthly "Made in Singapore" campaigns at its own costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It needs the Government, other companies and consumers to join in enhancing our food security.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry support the efforts of companies, such as FairPrice, to build our local production capacity?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The quality of soil and climate used to determine agricultural yield.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Now, a technologically driven ecosystem can level the playing field.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the Netherlands is small and densely populated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It does not have most of the resources necessary for large-scale agriculture.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, it is the globe's No 2 exporter of food measured by value, second only to the US.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For a sense of its achievements, the US is 270 times its land mass.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What Silicon Valley has done for the US' information technology (IT) industry, Food Valley has achieved the same for Dutch agriculture.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Wageningen University and Research (WUR) is a crucible of innovative re-cultural developments, not unlike what the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Alumni have done in the IT world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While we might not be able to go to such a scale as the Dutch, we can be the crucible of change in development in our region.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Its areas include R&D and logistics, urban farming, agriculture and aquaculture financing and insurance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our ambitions must now match the urgency and enormity of Singapore's food security challenge.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If we can grow the industry, this will mean tremendous opportunities for the economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What is the total economic value we can generate if we reach our target local production?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How many and what types of jobs can we expect to create?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can only grow our agriculture industry if we have the right capital and political will.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Viable businesses ultimately determine the sustainability of the industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry ensure that there are sufficient capital and skilled manpower in the system to drive the growth of startups?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Netherlands' WUR and its impact on agricultural innovation suggest that we need to invest in our local academia.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to marry the science with the market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How does the Ministry plan to jumpstart and develop this field in the Institutes of Higher Learning?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even as we grow the local content of our production, our legislation must be kept market-friendly without compromising our food safety.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The food supply chain is fraught with risks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: From cultivation and harvesting, things can easily go wrong.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Without a doubt, this consolidation of regulatory oversight for food safety and security under a single agency will be more efficient.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The streamlining of processes and the sharing of facilities and technology will enable all the various teams to communicate more effectively, reduce red tape, avoid duplication and work more productively.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But for all the work behind the scenes, what are the benefits for Singaporeans and companies from this consolidation?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Minister share some examples of how these changes translate to, for example, the ability to conduct more accurate tests and frequent checks, or shorten approval times for certain applications, among others?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As with any transition, there will be unexpected issues which will crop up.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With less than a month to go before the start of SFA on 1 April, what are some of the challenges, if any, which the agencies involved encounter and how are these problems being solved?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Rising temperatures pose a particular threat to food safety in Singapore, for example, as our wet markets and hawker centres are not air-conditioned, exposing all food to higher risks of spoilage.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is the Ministry's view on this problem?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With climate change, we can expect more unpredictable and intense rainfall.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What are some of PUB's plans to mitigate flood risks in the face of this challenge?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry share some updates, starting with the progress of the various drainage improvement works, canals, retention and any new detention tanks around our island?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How many and where are these works being done and what are the expected dates of completion?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand that last year alone, the Ministry received about 500 submissions for plans to build retention tanks.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But as of February 2018, only 158 have been completed.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is the status now for these projects?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Besides these constructions, the maintenance of our drains is equally important.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: From the regular inspections, what common problems were detected and how can members of the public assist to keep obstructions out of the drains?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And lastly, as I also called for last year, would the Ministry be considering the use of innovative porous materials, such as durable permeable concrete on our roads and walkways to facilitate drainage?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Water conservation is key to ensuring sustainability of our water supply.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: The study also found that even amongst those willing to conserve water, many said that they did not have the means to manage water consumption effectively.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: So, what are the initiatives to assist businesses in managing their water demand and increasing water efficiency?

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Mr Chairman, may I have your permission to use slides to accompany my speech, please?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As a small island state, Singapore's survival and success is a miracle.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Yet, we were determined to build a successful, thriving and liveable home and by pursuing sustainable development from the word "go".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We overcame our challenges through two key approaches.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Even as the Government tackled current problems, it scanned the horizon for threats and opportunities and planned decades ahead; decades, not years.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Second, the ability to implement policies and plans effectively.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Faced with a challenge, we start small, learn from others, harness technology, invest in R&D and keep on trying until we get it right.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Then, we take our solutions and scale up to benefit the whole nation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In doing so, we also grow our enterprises and create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is the essence of our Water Story.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We now welcome the Singapore Food Agency into our MEWR family.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is with the same understanding that food security is an existential issue, just like water, that we are writing our Singapore Food Story.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But first, Mr Chairman, let me dwell on our Water Story.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Since Independence, there has been the perception that water could be used as leverage against Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, there have been threats to cut off our water supply.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It was against this backdrop of needing to ensure the security and resilience of Singapore's water supply that we set out to create drinking water from used water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It took us more than two decades before we were ready to scale up production of NEWater.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We built a demonstration plant, started water quality measurement programmes, and rallied the entire nation's support.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is a feat to be proud of that we have integrated our used water into the water system into a closed loop, safely and reliably.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Drugs disposed of in sinks or toilets will be substantially removed through the water reclamation process.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our NEWater technology is so reliable that the Reverse Osmosis process will effectively remove any remaining pharmaceutical compounds when treated used water is channelled into the NEWater production.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB's constant monitoring showed that pharmaceutical compounds were not detected in our drinking water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I hope that will put to rest Ms Irene Quay's concerns about PUB's treatment capabilities in removing drugs from used water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Every time I describe to an international audience how we, as a nation, drink and use water from this system with full confidence of its safety and hygiene, I cannot help but beam with pride.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Today, NEWater is a national tap that is recognised internationally for its high quality and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about new developments in the water sector.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We already have the electro-deionisation technology that can potentially halve the energy required today in conventional reverse osmosis desalination.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are ready to scale up and deploy this technology at one of the process trains in PUB's Tuas Desalination Plant from 2020.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The gains from R&D go beyond solving our water problems.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Over the years, we have developed a thriving water industry, with over 200 companies and more than 25 R&D centres.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Singapore is now one of the best and busiest hydrohubs where companies come to prove their patents and scalability in a live water system.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our R&D efforts also allow PUB to grow our local enterprises when it partners the industry to develop innovative solutions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB worked with them to develop an early warning system that detects illegal discharge of heavy metals into the sewerage system.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: EnvironSens has already attracted investments to manufacture and market their products in countries, such as the US, China and India.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have come a long way in our Water Story, but we cannot rest on our laurels.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Climate change is bringing new and wicked problems.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is no coincidence that we are building more desalination and NEWater plants.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We need to produce water almost at will, regardless of whether the rains will come.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: On the other hand, climate change also brings more frequent intense storms, which could mean more floods, as noted by Dr Chia Shi-Lu.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As a low-lying island, Singapore is particularly vulnerable to sea level rise that can exacerbate flooding problems.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Members may have seen the Straits Times' interactive graphic that shows "Singapore Underwater".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That is already a reality in the Pacific Ocean where at least eight islands have disappeared under the sea.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Upgrading works at two major waterways, the Bukit Timah First Diversion Canal and Sungei Pandan Kechil, will be completed this year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will commence drainage upgrading works at another 16 locations this year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As Er Dr Lee Bee Wah noted, climate change must be tackled at regional and global platforms.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In the meantime, we must press on to transform our economy towards a low carbon future and do our part for the planet.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will step up solar adoption, as highlighted by Miss Cheng Li Hui.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Economic Development Board (EDB) is also exploring the possibility of a commercial floating solar system at Kranji Reservoir.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are also exploring such floating PV systems off Singapore's coast, as well as integrating solar PV into our building facades to maximise solar energy generation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Promoting sustainable transport and managing vehicular emissions are also key.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked about our plans to manage transport emissions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We promote cleaner vehicles through emissions standards and encourage the early replacement of older and more pollutive vehicles, such as through the Early Turnover Scheme.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: More than 40,000 commercial diesel vehicles have switched to cleaner vehicles under this scheme.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We also work with MOT to encourage adoption of cleaner vehicles, and regularly engage the industry, such as commercial electric vehicle fleet owners like HDT and BlueSG, on their plans.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As one of my colleagues, a Minister of Environment, quipped, "There is a link between carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: You aim for cleaner vehicles to solve pollution, you will also solve greenhouse gases that will help with climate change." The preceding examples are what we all call climate mitigation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Government is also planning ahead to protect Singapore against climate change impacts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about our initiatives to build climate resilience.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: My colleagues in the Ministry of National Development (MND) spoke at length on this.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To guide our policies in fortifying Singapore against climate change, we must build up our knowledge of climate science.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, because there is limited literature on climate change effects in the tropics, we can lead.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is why we set up the Centre for Climate Research Singapore (CCRS) in 2013.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are stepping up investments to build capability in CCRS and the local scientific community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This year, CCRS will embark on the National Sea Level Programme to better understand sea levels around Singapore so that we can develop robust projections and plans for the long term.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Chairman, we will also press on to ensure water security.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Work on the Deep Tunnel Sewerage System Phase 2 (DTSS2) is on track.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will continue to build up our desalination and NEWater capacities to ensure that our water supply is secure and resilient in the long term.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Water security is an existential issue for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will continue to do what it takes to ensure it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As updated previously in this House, we have been closely monitoring developments and will not allow our water security to be compromised.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are concerned that TPL has been unable to fulfil various contractual obligations, in particular, by failing to keep the plant reliably operational as required.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In addition, TPL has not been able to produce financial evidence to demonstrate its ability to keep the plant running for the next six months.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Hence, PUB has decided to exercise its rights under its contract with TPL and initiate the necessary proceedings to safeguard the continued operations of the plant.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This action is to safeguard our water security.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Over the past five decades, we have worked hard to diversify our water resources and build up our four national taps.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We saw how the Linggiu Reservoir stock level plummeted to 20% in 2016.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It has yet to recover fully even after more than two years.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: While stock levels had gradually increased to 72% by end 2018, after just two months this year, it has dropped again to 64%.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That is why our weather-resilient NEWater and desalination taps are integral to our water security.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Chairman, even as we secure our water supply, we cannot ignore water conservation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In Qatar, where water is provided for free, daily consumption is around 500 litres per person.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In Singapore, we have worked hard to embed water conservation in our national DNA.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our domestic water consumption decreased from 148 litres per capita per day in 2016, to 141 litres in 2018.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But we agree with Mr Amrin Amin that we must do more, to reach our goal of 130 litres by 2030.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To this end, we will help consumers make more informed purchasing decisions, such as through the Mandatory Water Efficiency Labelling Scheme.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Similarly, for the non-domestic sector, PUB is working with the Singapore Environment Council to develop a Green Labelling Scheme for commercial equipment, such as commercial dishwashers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB also supports businesses through its Water Efficiency Fund.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Last weekend, President Halimah officiated Singapore World Water Day, marking the start of a year-long conservation campaign.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: PUB is launching the inaugural #GoBlue4SG movement, to rally the community and celebrate our collective actions to conserve water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: One of the highlights – City Turns Blue – will see more than 20 buildings light up Singapore's skyline on 22 March.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I am heartened that over 150 schools will undertake water rationing exercises to drive home the value of water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I encourage all of us to "Make Every Drop Count".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The impact of climate change goes beyond water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, the destinies of two other agencies under my Ministry – environment and food – are also tied to the impacts of climate change, like water.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Resource scarcity is set to become the new normal.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: And with it, cascading impacts, such as disruptions to supply chains that fuel our economies, and increased risk of global conflict.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We must, therefore, apply a strategic lens to Singapore's resource resilience.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As I mentioned in my opening remarks, to meet this new challenge of securing our food and other resources, we can apply the lessons from our Water Story.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We want to break away from the linear economy, where we take, make, use and toss without a second thought, because this is not sustainable.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Therefore, we must make a paradigm shift towards circular economy approaches.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Beyond protecting the planet, circular economy approaches can enable Singapore to overcome resource constraints and strengthen overall resilience.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many may not realise this, but NEWater embodies the circular economy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We use a resource, in this case water, for as long as possible, and ensure that what can be reused is put back into the system.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This shirt, which I received recently at the Special ASEAN Ministerial Meeting on Marine Debris this week, is another good example of the circular economy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It says there that this polo shirt is recycled from 12 bottles, polyethylene terephthalate bottles (PET) bottles that all of us use.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But I would encourage most of us to use reuseable bottles instead.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In essence, what they have done is try to keep using what we have within our systems and not toss it away, in this case, into the sea.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This same thinking applies to every other resource, for example, lithium-ion batteries found in almost all our electronics – handphones, laptops and even electric vehicles.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Global demand is soaring, but mineral sources for lithium, cobalt and coltan are finite and costly to mine.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Continuously exploiting these minerals may harm the gorillas that Mr Louis Ng was talking about.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: But we can collect these used uncontaminated e-wastes in meaningful amounts and apply R&D and new technologies to extract the precious minerals.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This will increase our resource resilience and avoid harming the environment.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Businesses are alive to the opportunities of the circular economy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Among them is our own homegrown e-waste recycling company, Total Environmental Solutions (TES).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: TES recovers treasures from trash, extracting gold, silver and palladium from e-waste.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: TES has plans to expand its lithium-ion battery treatment process facility.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Recyclers like TES are important as they ensure that heavy metals from e-waste do not contaminate our environment but are instead recovered as valuable resources to power our economy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This will also help to extend the lifespan of Semakau Landfill, as Miss Cheng Li Hui highlighted.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To do so, we need to invest in R&D, in close partnership with industry and research institutions, just like how we have grown our water industry and research ecosystem to tackle our water challenge.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This will allow us to overcome technological barriers in our drive towards a zero-waste nation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Promising projects include Singapore Polytechnic’s development of green chemistry technology to recover precious metals in e-waste, and Nanyang Technological University’s method to rapidly convert food waste into high grade bio-fertilisers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The result of such R&D means more opportunities for our enterprises and, consequently, more jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Another company that has seized such opportunities is Westcom Solutions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Westcom got its researchers to help improve processes, to scale up and transition from being a company that distributes food waste digesters to one that manufactures them.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I look forward to the day when our stores carry home food digesters that are compact, economical and easy to use, something we can put in our own homes, to convert our food waste into compost to grow plants and even food at home.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This also reduces the need to transport food waste across the island and keep our waste system free from pests!

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As R&D powers our enterprises and creates new opportunities for them, it will also create new jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We need engineers to develop standards for waste management and recycling operations, scientists to study micro-organisms for efficient food waste processing, and analysts to study the data created and create strategies for scaling up.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will also partner other agencies and the industry to turn trash into treasure through circular economy strategies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The facilities will house multiple recyclers and be located close to other industries.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This will present opportunities to reuse waste materials and other industrial by-products, thereby closing resource loops at the local level.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are studying how we can turn incineration ash into construction materials, instead of landfilling it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: NEA has appointed industry players to demonstrate their technologies, with plans to start field trials next year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will take careful steps though, as two-thirds of Singapore is water catchment that must remain free from pollution.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Building a circular economy also requires international cooperation, as value chains are interconnected.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Singapore will play a constructive role in this process.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We supported the Special ASEAN Ministerial Meeting on Marine Debris two days ago, where ASEAN countries agreed to advance concrete actions on the circular economy, the same conference where Thailand gave delegates this T-shirt to demonstrate the potential of the circular economy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will continue cooperating with our partners in the region to work towards zero waste.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Chairman, let me now turn to food, another essential resource.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Singapore is also exposed to the volatilities of the global food market, because we import over 90% of our food.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Just last year, Malaysia announced that it was considering limiting exports of eggs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked how the SFA's formation will benefit Singaporeans and companies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: SFA’s mission is to ensure and secure a supply of safe food for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As the lead agency to strengthen food safety and security, SFA will have regulatory oversight across the entire food chain, from farm-to-fork.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It will also partner businesses to transform our agri-food industry and create, again, good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked about SFA’s plans to strengthen our food security.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: SFA will pursue three broad strategies called the three food baskets – "Diversify Import Sources"; "Grow Local" and "Grow Overseas" – which I talked about during the Second Reading of the SFA Bill.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Today, I would like to focus on our "Grow Local" strategy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is an ambitious multi-fold increase to our current production.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Remember, we import over 90% of our food?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To get to the "30 by 30 vision" will require our agri-food industry to adopt new solutions to raise productivity, apply R&D, strengthen climate resilience and overcome our resource constraints.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We need new paradigms in the agri-food industry.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Supporting our existing farms to innovate and increase productivity is a key pillar of the "Grow Local" strategy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many of these farms are household names which produce eggs, vegetables and fish.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, vegetable farms Kok Fah and Ho Ka Clean have been feeding Singapore for over 20 years.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Agriculture Productivity Fund (APF) has supported them to integrate climate control and automation into their operations, thereby raising their capacity and productivity.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will similarly work with our existing coastal fish farms.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Singapore Aquaculture Technologies was one of the first coastal fish farms to adopt closed containment aquaculture systems.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This protects fish production from sea-borne threats, such as algae blooms or oil spills.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: More than 90 farms have benefited from APF, and I encourage all our farms to tap on it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will also expand production in state-of-the-art indoor farms.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Farms, such as Sustenir and Panasonic, optimise plant growth and increase yield exponentially through high-tech solutions like LED lighting and climate control.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: By controlling growing variables, these farms are climate-resilient and can maintain high quality.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We expect to see more such farms as successful tenderers in the recent agricultural land tender exercises begin production and scale up.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Farmers of the future will operate computerised control systems in a pleasant environment.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: SFA will also support the growing interest in urban farming, such as on rooftops.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This brings the community together, and attunes Singaporeans to food security, by involving them directly in food production.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our plans to "Grow Local" also extend to productive and sustainable fish farming.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our vision is to develop Singapore into a tropical aquaculture hub, much like how we have the hydrohub.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: One area we are studying is deep sea fish farming, which can contribute significantly to local production.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: A local first mover is Barramundi Asia, which uses large sea cages to culture Asian seabass in the deep waters off Pulau Semakau, our landfill.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I recently visited them and was impressed by their fish vaccination process.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: SFA will work with agencies and the industry to open up more sites for deep sea farming with deep technology.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Thus, R&D will be the key driver, again, to help us achieve our "30 by 30" vision, grow our enterprises and, consequently, create good jobs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will grow an ecosystem of R&D players to support agri- and aquaculture industry developments.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: SFA’s Marine Aquaculture Centre will contribute to this effort by sharing its expertise and providing facilities for R&D.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked how we will prepare Singaporeans for the growing opportunities in the agri-food sector.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The agri-food industry will require a workforce with good understanding of urban food production processes and business models, and multidisciplinary expertise in science, engineering, info-communications and more.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: ELP will emplace ITE graduates in industry and equip them with the knowledge and skills to become agriculture and aquaculture technicians.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will also partner universities to groom agri- and aqua-technologists and culturists, urban farming specialists and researchers to meet future needs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Like every sector in Singapore, the agri-food sector must embrace sustainability.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Some of our farms are already employing circular economy principles.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indoor farm Sustenir is using carbon dioxide, a by-product from the petrochemical industry, to enhance vegetable yields.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: N&N, a layer egg farm, carries out bio-digestion using poultry waste to produce energy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is then used to dry by-products from the food manufacturing industry to produce chicken feed.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These examples show that what we see as waste in one sector can be feedstock for another.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will do more to find synergies across different systems, such as food, water, energy and waste, and then scale them up for commercial viability.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will apply the circular economy approach across systems to achieve zero waste and to lower use of resources.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This requires an ambitious R&D programme, integrated upfront planning and design and close collaboration with the industry.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is the future economy, and the Government will invest significant resources to enable Singaporeans to thrive in it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These significant investments will help us to explore greater possibilities across the food-water-energy-waste nexus, achieve new results, and scale up.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: One early success is NEA and PUB’s successful trial at Ulu Pandan Water Reclamation Plant.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It has proven that co-digesting food waste and used water sludge can triple biogas yield, compared to treating the used water sludge alone.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The biogas is used to generate energy for the facility.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Chairman, the plans we have for the water, food and environmental sectors will open up a variety of exciting opportunities for our enterprises and jobs in our industries.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We hope to produce more of the likes of EnvironSens, TES, Sustenir and Barramundi Asia.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will also need many people with diverse interests and skills to help us tackle our challenges.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Ahmad Zaki Bin Salleh and Ms Rajakumar Amritha are at the forefront of our efforts to enhance food resilience and ensure water security.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Ahmad Zaki, a senior engineer with PUB, oversaw the planning and construction of the Stamford Detention Tank, while Amritha contributes to the smooth operations at Woodleigh Waterworks.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Ms Marie Tan and Mr Lee Yuan Hao are part of our growing agri-food sector to strengthen food security.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Marie oversees fish health at Barramundi Asia’s nursery while Yuan Hao founded Ding He Agriculture, a vertical indoor agri-farming firm.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Ms Jade Loh and Mr Heng Kim Soon are contributing to our Zero Waste Cause.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Jade and her team at Plaspulp Union Pte Ltd explore recycling solutions for complex waste materials, while Kim Soon conducts R&D on uses for incineration ash.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Together with their colleagues in the water, food and environmental sectors, these young people will see our plans through in the decades to come.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Chairman, climate change will bring new existential threats, but also exciting opportunities.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We must do as our forefathers did: stay alert and nimble and continue to plan and prepare for the long term.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It took us more than two decades to create NEWater.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I now hand over to the Senior Minister of State Amy Khor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Chairman, in 2018, which was designated the Year of Climate Action, we rallied individuals and organisations and received more than 340,000 climate action pledges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Collectively, our people, public and private (3P) partners initiated and organised more than 800 climate action events.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: That is more than two events a day!

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: It shows the far-reaching impact of consultation and partnership.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To build on this momentum, we designated 2019 as the Year Towards Zero Waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Master Plan will cover our three priority waste streams of e-waste, packaging waste, including plastics and food waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We hope that it will align the 3P sectors and the research and development community towards a common vision of a Zero Waste Nation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Master Plan brings together our collective efforts over several years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Last year alone, NEA consulted more than 250 companies on measures to address our priority waste streams.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: NEA has also approved two Environmental Services Regulatory Sandbox applications since it was launched in July 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These efforts help us to co-create our regulations with the industry, ensuring we minimise business costs and enhance sustainable economic growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
